title: TLS and secure connections
subtitle: Learn what TLS protects, how a client decides to trust a server, and how to stop certificate expiry from taking your service down.

TLS does two jobs: it agrees on secret keys, and it proves the server holds the private key for a certificate the client trusts. The outages in this lesson were not about cryptography. They were about a certificate that expired. A chain the client cannot follow fails the same way.
Step through one TLS 1.3 handshake and a request. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
The TLS 1.3 handshake in plain words
TLS runs on top of a
The client sends the options it supports and its part of a key exchange (a "key share")
The server picks the options and sends its own key share. From here, both sides can compute the same keys. Every handshake message after ServerHello is encrypted
The server sends its certificate chain. It also sends a signature over the whole handshake, made with the private key that matches the certificate
. A thief who copied the certificate but not the private key cannot make this signature.
The client checks everything and sends Finished. Now application data can flow
This takes one round trip, so
How the client checks the chain
The client must check that the certificate is for the host it asked for
. It then follows the chain. Each certificate must be signed by the next one up, and the top must be signed by a trust anchor, such as a root in the trust store
. Each certificate must be valid now: the current time must be inside its dates
When the server sends its own certificate plus the intermediate, the client can check every signature up to a root it already trusts. It does not need to download anything else
If the check fails, an automated client must log the error and should close the connection

Every certificate has an end date

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: Keep a list of every certificate: where it lives, who owns it, and when it expires. Shared certificates for many names make one expiry hit many services.
"What renews it, and what tells us when renewal fails?"
Alert on the renewal, not only on the date.
pager, 30 days and 7 days ahead. A chat channel is not enough.
Check certificates from outside too, with a probe that follows the full chain like a real client.
When one client fails and another works, compare the chain each one receives and the trust store each one uses.
Turn off 0-RTT for APIs that change data, unless every request is safe to replay.
Never ship code that disables certificate checks, even "only in staging".
"Write a script that lists every TLS certificate on these 40 hosts, with issuer, names and expiry date. Sort by expiry and flag anything under 30 days."

q.v: What does TLS give you on a connection?

options.v: Encryption, protection against changes, and proof of the server's identity.
Proof that the user is logged in.

why.v: TLS 1.3 gives confidentiality, integrity, and authentication. The server is always authenticated. The client is only authenticated if the server asks.

q.v: Why is 0-RTT data risky for a "POST /payments" request?

options.v: An attacker can capture it and send it again, and TLS does not stop replays across connections.
It is slower than a normal handshake.

why.v: RFC 9846 says there are no guarantees of non-replay between connections. RFC 8470 says clients must not send unsafe methods in early data.

q.v: Your certificate renewal runs from a cron job every 60 days. Your CA moves to 45-day certificates. What happens?

options.v: Certificates expire before the job runs, and clients get errors.
The CA renews the certificates for you.

why.v: Let's Encrypt warns that fixed schedules like 60 days will fail. Use ACME Renewal Information, or renew about two thirds of the way through the lifetime.

q.v: Your load balancer ends TLS and sends plain HTTP to your servers. What is true?

options.v: Traffic is encrypted all the way to the server.
Traffic is encrypted only to the load balancer. Inside, it is readable unless you add TLS to the servers too.
TLS cannot be ended at a load balancer.

why.v: AWS says an HTTPS listener decrypts requests before it sends them on. For encryption to the server, use HTTPS to the targets, or a Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener.

q.v: A website sends the HSTS header. What happens next time a user types http:// for it?

options.v: The browser changes it to https:// before it sends anything.
The browser shows a warning and lets the user choose.

why.v: HSTS tells browsers to turn insecure links to that host into secure ones, and not to let users click through certificate errors.
